Generally yeah, but depends on what you're trying to accomplish.

Benefits of putting them on the ground:
Faster decomposition and nutrient return to soil
Creates habitat for ground-dwelling insects, salamanders, small mammals
Improves moisture retention in soil
Builds up forest duff layer
Reduces fuel ladder for potential fires (dead branches high up are more dangerous)

What you might lose:
Cavity-nesting birds and bats use standing dead branches
Some insects specifically need standing deadwood
Natural pruning process (branches fall when ready)

Practical approach for your situation:
Since you said it's crowded and branches are hanging on each other, breaking the obviously dead/dangerous stuff and laying it on the ground is fine - you're just speeding up what would happen naturally in the next windstorm anyway.

Focus on:
Stuff that's clearly dead and hanging precariously
Lower branches creating fire ladder danger
Branches blocking pathways or creating hazards

Leave:
Larger dead standing trunks (snags) - these are premium wildlife habitat
Stuff that's still solidly attached and not a hazard

Lay them perpendicular to slopes if you're on a hill - slows water, reduces erosion, traps organic matter.
The forest will use whatever you give it.

So what I'm trying to do is food forestry optimize for food production of a forest

For food forestry, yes - clear that dead stuff aggressively.

Why clearing helps food production:
Light penetration: Dead hanging branches shade your productive understory.

Even cleared canopy needs to let dappled light through for berries, hazelnuts, fruiting shrubs
Air circulation: Crowded dead branches trap humidity and reduce airflow = fungal disease pressure on your productive plants
Pathogen reduction: Dead wood hanging around can harbor pests/diseases that jump to your productive species
Access: You need to actually get to your food - paths, harvesting space, management access
Competition: Dead stuff still takes up space that could be occupied by productive layers

Food forest approach to clearing:
Remove dead branches, especially at human height and below (that's your productive zone)
Thin canopy selectively to create light pockets for sun-loving producers (pawpaw, persimmon, hazelnuts need some light)
Keep some standing dead wood at edges for beneficial insects/pollinators
Lay cleared material as hugelkultur-style mounds or paths - don't just scatter it
Big logs can become mushroom cultivation logs (shiitake, oyster)

Strategic placement of debris:
Borders of clearings (wildlife/insect habitat)
Paths/walkways (weed suppression, slow traffic)
Swales/water capture (if you're doing water harvesting)
Mushroom cultivation zones

You're basically converting wild forest ecology to managed productive ecology.
Different goals = different rules.

Parenting is almost entirely flexibility and adaptation.
You can have principles and general strategies, but specific plans rarely survive contact with reality.
Wrestling example: You had a solid plan - one defensive foundation, one offensive move, three attempts.
But between now and the meet, Charlie might get sick, the coach might change the bracket, she might face someone way bigger, or she might just forget everything the second she steps on the mat.
The adaptation skill is: maintain the goal (have fun, try the move), but be ready to completely pivot on execution.
Maybe she's too nervous and just needs "have fun and don't quit.
" Maybe she's crushing it and needs "try something new.
" Maybe the move doesn't work and you say "great sprawl, that counts as trying.

"

The parents who struggle most are the ones who can't let go of THE PLAN when the kid or situation changes.
The flexible ones are like "okay, new information, new approach, same underlying values.

"

You're building this muscle constantly - meal planning (kid suddenly hates pasta), schedules (practice cancelled), discipline (what worked last month doesn't work now), education (they're not learning the way you thought).
The core stays stable.
The tactics are water.

Free speech protects expressing ideas, not pure disruption.
In public spaces, you have strong First Amendment protections, but they're not absolute.

The line is roughly:

Protected:
Yelling numbers as protest ("This numbering system is dehumanizing!

")
Standing with a sign criticizing Costco
Chanting slogans that happen to disrupt
Offensive speech expressing viewpoint (Cohen v.

California - "Fuck the Draft")

Not protected:
Yelling random numbers *purely to cause chaos*
Creating a disturbance without communicating an idea
Blocking access to public facilities
Inciting immediate lawless action (Brandenburg test)
True threats

Why your example likely fails protection:

Disorderly conduct laws in most states prohibit intentionally causing "public inconvenience, annoyance, alarm" through conduct that serves no legitimate purpose.

The key is content vs. conduct:
If you're yelling numbers to make a point about surveillance culture or whatever = speech
If you're yelling numbers just to fuck with people = conduct

Courts apply "time, place, manner" restrictions - governments can regulate HOW you speak (volume, location, timing) as long as restrictions are:
Content-neutral
Narrowly tailored
Leave alternative channels open

Real-world outcome: Even in a public space doing your number-yelling, you'd likely get hit with disorderly conduct, disturbing the peace, or similar charges.
Your defense would be "I was expressing political protest" and success depends on whether you can articulate what idea you were communicating.

The "veneer of protest" question is smart though:

Even in PUBLIC spaces where First Amendment applies, courts aren't idiots.

They ask:
Are you actually communicating an idea?

- Or are you just causing disruption and labeling it protest?

Test cases:
Burning flag = protected (Texas v.

Johnson) - clear political message

Your defense needs to articulate WHAT you're protesting and HOW the conduct expresses that

The real distinction:
Pure expressive conduct (kneeling during anthem, wearing armband) = protected
Conduct that happens to involve words but serves no expressive purpose (yelling fire, calling random numbers) = not protected

Courts use reasonableness test.
If a reasonable person couldn't identify your message, it's just disruption.

Exactly - almost never contested because the stakes are too low and enforcement is discretionary.

Here's the reality check:

Why it's rarely tested:
Most people comply when told to stop/leave
Cop discretion filters out 95% of cases ("just move along, buddy")
Prosecutors drop minor nuisance charges - not worth their time
Fighting a $50-200 disorderly conduct ticket costs thousands in legal fees
You need ACLU-level backing to make it a constitutional case

Who actually contests these:
Mass protest arrests (where org funds defense)
Street preachers with backing from religious freedom orgs
Performers/buskers fighting for right to public space
Cases with clear political salience where advocacy groups see test case potential

The selective enforcement reality:
Nuisance laws are *incredibly broad* on paper, giving cops massive discretion.

In practice:
White guy protesting property taxes?
"Sir, please move along.

"
Black Lives Matter blocking intersection?
Mass arrests, charges stick.

The lack of contesting isn't because the law is clear - it's because:
Fighting costs more than complying
Most violations are genuinely disruptive without real speech value
System filters out edge cases through discretion before they hit court

So yeah, nuisance law theoretically constrains lots of speech, practically it's only enforced/contested when someone either (a) really pisses off authorities, (b) has organizational backing to make it a test case.
